whyThisMatters: Most incidents do not start with hacking. They start with someone opening the wrong message. Today you will practise noticing the small details that give a fake away, whatever your role.
rememberThis: One habit: pause for ten seconds before you click or tap. Stop, Verify through a channel you already trust (a known phone number or a saved bookmark), then Report anything suspicious to IT.

discussionPrompts: Ask which detail people noticed first: the sender address, the urgent wording, or the attachment name? Would they check the same thing on their phone?
For the link card, ask how many people hover over (or press and hold) a link before they click. What makes that hard when you are busy?
Ask if anyone has seen a text, a pop-up or a flood of approval requests like the last three cards. What did they do?
facilitatorNotes.commonWrongAnswer: People often judge by which email looks neater. Real and fake look almost identical. The habit to build is to check the exact sender address and the web address letter by letter, not the logo or the body text.

items.title: Real vs Fake Job Offer Email
items.whatIsWrong: The fake email comes from hr@acmecorp-careers.com. The real one comes from hr@acmecorp.com. The sender domain (the part after the @) is different: the fake adds "-careers". The logo, subject and body look almost identical.
items.whyItsSuspicious: Anyone can copy a logo and wording, but they cannot send from your company's real domain. A small change in the domain is easy to miss when you are in a hurry, so read it letter by letter. The real domain is exactly acmecorp.com, with no hyphens or extra words. What to do: Stop, do not reply or open the attachment. Verify by calling HR on a number you already know. Report it to IT.

items.title: Real vs Fake Bank-Detail Change Email
items.whatIsWrong: The fake email says "URGENT — Bank Detail Change — Action Required TODAY" and warns that you will miss this month's payment run. It tells you to skip the normal approval steps and not to call back. The real email is calm: the payment is scheduled for 28 Nov, no immediate action is needed, and any bank change is checked by calling a known number.
items.whyItsSuspicious: Pressure is the tell. Attackers use deadlines and fear so you act before you think. A real supplier bank change never asks you to skip approval or avoid a call-back, even if the email looks right. What to do: Stop and do not pay. Verify by calling the supplier on a number already in your records, not one in the email. Report it to Finance and IT.

items.title: Real vs Fake Payslip Email
items.whatIsWrong: The fake email has attachments you did not expect. Payslip_March.pdf.exe ends in .exe, which means it is a program, not a PDF. Documents.zip is a generic archive with the password "1234" in the email. It also asks you to click "Enable Content". The real email has clearly named files: Payslip_Feb2025_SamLee.pdf and Team_Schedule_Feb-Apr.xlsx.
items.whyItsSuspicious: Attachments are a common way to install malware. Ask: did I expect this file, and does its name and type match? A payslip should be a PDF. A double ending like .pdf.exe, a password-protected ZIP, or a request to "Enable Content" or macros are warning signs. What to do: Stop and do not open it. Verify with HR Payroll on a known number or through the HR portal. Report the email to IT.

items.title: Real vs Fake Schedule Confirmation Email
items.whatIsWrong: Both emails show the same blue link text. In the fake, hovering over the link (or pressing and holding on a phone) shows the link preview, the real destination: https://portal-acmecorp-secure.net/staff/verify?id=42, plus a short link, http://bit.ly/AcmeSchedule-Confirm. The real email's link truly goes to portal.acmecorp.com. Both messages use the same name, so the name does not prove anything.
items.whyItsSuspicious: The text you see can say anything. Only the real destination matters. The fake domain is portal-acmecorp-secure.net, not acmecorp.com. Short links like bit.ly also hide where you will land. What to do: Stop before clicking and check the link preview. Verify by opening the portal from a bookmark you saved yourself. Report the email to IT if the preview does not match.

items.title: Real vs Fake Staff Portal Login
items.whatIsWrong: The fake login page shows the address "portal.acrnecorp.com" in the browser. The letters "rn" together look like an "m", so it reads as acmecorp at a glance. The real address is "portal.acmecorp.com". The login screens are otherwise identical.
items.whyItsSuspicious: Attackers can copy the look of a login page exactly, but not the real web address. A lookalike login page steals your password the moment you sign in. Check the address bar letter by letter before you type. What to do: Stop and do not enter your password. Verify by opening the portal from your own bookmark. Report the link to IT, and change your password if you already typed it.

items.title: Fake Delivery Text Message
items.whatIsWrong: A text message from "QuickParcel" says: "Your package could not be delivered. Verify your address within 2 hours to avoid return: bit.ly/quickparcel-verify-4x9". It comes from an unknown sender and uses a short link and a 2-hour deadline.
items.whyItsSuspicious: This is smishing: phishing by text message. The tells are the unexpected message, the short link that hides the real address, and the deadline that pushes you to act now. Phones show less detail, so it is easier to fall for. What to do: Stop and do not tap the link. Verify by checking the courier's real app or website, typed in yourself. Report the text (forward it to your IT team or mobile provider) and delete it.

items.title: Fake IT Support Pop-Up
items.whatIsWrong: A box pops up saying "Your PC has a critical error. Enter your password to allow IT to fix it remotely" with a SUBMIT PASSWORD button.
items.whyItsSuspicious: Real IT staff never ask for your password in a pop-up. This box is a trick to steal your login, dressed up as a system warning. What to do: Stop, close the box and type nothing. Verify by contacting the IT helpdesk through the number or ticket system you normally use. Report it, and on a shared computer tell the next user not to use it until IT has checked.

items.title: Repeated Login Approval Requests
items.whatIsWrong: Your phone shows many "Approve sign-in?" requests in under a minute that you did not start. These come from MFA (multi-factor authentication: the extra approval step after your password, like a code or an Approve button).
items.whyItsSuspicious: Many requests means someone already has your password and hopes you will tap Approve just to make it stop. This is called MFA fatigue. Even one unexpected request is a warning. What to do: Stop and tap Deny, never Approve. Verify nothing is wrong by changing your password from a device you trust. Report it to the IT helpdesk right away.
